docs.title: Tadirel — research notes
docs.text: This is the knowledge base behind Tadirel, a from-scratch client (backend + desktop app + Android app) that controls Tadiran/Gree air conditioners locally over LAN, built by reverse-engineering the official Tadiran consumer app and the public Gree AC protocol.

docs.title: Map
docs.text:
• App teardown — what's inside the official app: bundled vendor SDKs, native libraries, permissions, how it's built.
  • Asset inventory — exhaustive catalog of every native library and asset file, plus third-party SDK identifiers found.
  • LAN protocol — the wire protocol actually used to talk to the AC's WiFi module (UDP port 7000, AES-encrypted JSON). This is the protocol Tadirel's own backend uses.
  • Cloud API — what is and isn't known about the remote/cloud control path. Short version: not publicly documented, not reimplemented here.
  • Architecture — design of Tadirel's own backend/desktop/Android apps.
  • Library notes — quirks found in the greeclimate PyPI package while building against real hardware.

docs.title: tl;dr for someone who just wants to control their AC
docs.text:
1. Your AC units are already on your home WiFi (bound once via the official app or the unit's own setup flow — Tadirel does not redo WiFi/BLE pairing, only talks to units already on the network).
  2. Each unit listens on UDP port 7000 and speaks Gree's open, community documented "Gree+" LAN protocol — AES-encrypted JSON packets, no cloud account needed, nothing proprietary to Tadiran.
  3. Tadirel's backend scans your subnet for these units, lets you name them, and sends them commands (power, mode, temp, fan, swing, light, turbo, etc).
  4. The desktop app (Eel-based) and Android app (Chaquopy-based) are thin UIs over that one shared backend.
  5. Everything only works on the same LAN/subnet as the AC units. For control from outside the house, tunnel into the LAN (Tailscale/ WireGuard) rather than going through Tadiran's undocumented cloud — see Cloud API for why.

docs.title: Confirmed hardware/software facts
docs.text:
• Tadiran-branded AC units sold with the official app are rebranded Gree hardware. The app's native AC-control layer is literally Gree's own com.gree.greeplus.sdk library (unobfuscated class names found in the app's bytecode) plus a native libgree.so.
  • The wire protocol property keys found in the app binary (Pow, Mod, SetTem, WdSpd, Lig, Tur, SwingLfRig, SwUpDn, Blo, Health, SwhSlp, StHt, SvSt, TemUn, TemRec) are byte-for-byte identical to the public, community reverse-engineered Gree LAN protocol (tomikaa87/gree-remote, cmroche/greeclimate), which is what Tadirel's backend uses.
  • Live-verified: 4 real units discovered and controlled on a home LAN — scan, status read, and a real power/light on→off round trip all confirmed against actual hardware.

docs.title: App teardown — official Tadiran consumer app
docs.text: Target: the official Tadiran air-conditioner control app for Android, analyzed at a recent release (React Native, Hermes engine, targetSdk 35-class build). Specifics below describe the app at the time of this research; app updates may change any of it.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Decompiled the Android package with jadx for class listing and resource IDs.
  • Decoded the binary AndroidManifest.xml with androguard (androguard.core.axml.AXMLPrinter) to read permissions and components.
  • Extracted every literal string from classes*.dex to find class names, URLs, and protocol constants.
  • The React Native JS bundle is compiled Hermes bytecode, not plain JS text — a plain strings dump over it merges adjacent string-table entries with no delimiter and produces garbage. hermes-dec (PyPI, by P1Security) parses the bytecode properly and exposes a clean, correctly delimited string list:
from hermes_dec.parsers.hbc_file_parser import HBCReader

with open("index.android.bundle", "rb") as f:
    reader = HBCReader()
    reader.read_whole_file(f)
# reader.strings -> list[str], tens of thousands of entries

!!! note "Tooling gotcha" hbctool (another PyPI Hermes disassembler) only supports older bytecode versions and fails outright on recent Hermes builds. hermes-dec handles the current version fine.

docs.title: App architecture
docs.text: React Native app packaged as a standard Android/Gradle project, bundling two third-party vendor SDKs for device control:

docs.title: 1. Gree's own SDK — com.gree.greeplus.sdk.*
docs.text:
This is the one that matters for AC control. Class names are not obfuscated — this is a third-party AAR dropped in whole:

  • GreePlusSdk — top-level SDK entry point.
  • Interface/IDeviceManager, Interface/IAPIManger, Interface/OnAPIRequestListener, Interface/OnModDevListener, Interface/OnScanDeviceListener, Interface/OnSocketListener, Interface/OnUnBindHomeDevListener, Interface/LinkConfigListener, Interface/GreeLinkConfigListener, Interface/OnWiFiScanListener — cloud API + local device management callbacks.
  • apcfg/IApConfigModel — classic AP-mode / SmartConfig WiFi provisioning (how a brand-new unit gets joined to WiFi the first time).
  • blecfg/BleConfig, blecfg/core/BleCommunicator, blecfg/core/BleScanner, blecfg/core/ConnectManager — BLE-based provisioning path (newer units support BLE setup too).
  • bean/BindDeviceBean, bean/BindDeviceResultBean, bean/QueryStateResultBean, bean/ModHomeDeviceBean, bean/ScanDeviceBean, bean/SyncHomeDeviceBean, bean/UserInfoBean, bean/WlanInfoPackBean — the usual bind/scan/query request/response DTOs.
  • util/AESUtil, util/AesCbcHelper, util/MD5Util, util/BytesHexStringTranslate — crypto helpers for the pack protocol.
  • util/BasePackCmd, util/DoorCmd — command-packet builders (DoorCmd implies the same SDK is reused by Gree for smart locks, not AC-specific).
  • corelib/CoreLib — likely the JNI bridge into native code.

Literal protocol property-key strings found directly in the string pool (survived obfuscation because they're JSON keys/data, not identifiers): Pow, Lig, Tur. These match the Gree LAN protocol exactly — see LAN protocol.

A native library libgree.so (~340 KB) ships alongside the Java classes. Its strings show only compiler/toolchain banners — no literal URLs or API paths, consistent with it being the AES/crypto primitive implementation rather than the networking layer.

docs.title: 2. Tuya's SDK (rebranded "ThingClips") — com.thingclips.smart.*
docs.text:
Much heavier footprint than Gree's SDK by string-reference count. The app sells other smart-home categories under the same account (a DoorCmd- adjacent scope suggests locks/sensors, not just AC). Bundled native libs include Tuya's link/security/MMKV/Matter-support libraries.

Not used by this project — the AC units this research targeted are confirmed Gree-protocol devices. If a Tadiran AC doesn't respond to a Gree-protocol UDP scan, it may be on this stack instead (Tuya's local/cloud protocol is a different, equally-documented ecosystem — see tinytuya/localtuya).

docs.title: 3. The app's own backend
docs.text:
This app is a white-label platform, not Tadiran-only

The bundle contains a complete onboarding flow for Ferroli, a different HVAC brand (FerroliConnectFirstScreen, FerroliConnectSecondScreen, ferroliConnectScreen:step1_*/step2_* translation keys). Tadiran's app is one brand's skin on a backend/app platform shared across vendors, not a Tadiran-specific build.

  • https://api.tadiran-iot.co.il — the app's own account/device-layer backend. A second, deeper pass over the Hermes string table (see Cloud API for the full breakdown) recovered real REST path prefixes (/tadiran-mobile-app/api/v1, /tadiran-mobile-app/api/v2, /mobile-app/api/v1, /eu/management/api/v1) and dozens of resource paths (/devices/, /user/, /shared-users/, /models/ai/recognize/, etc.), though the host and path prefixes were never observed concatenated as a single literal, so the exact pairing is inferred, not directly confirmed.
  • AWS Cognito identifiers, recovered from the native (dex) string pool rather than the JS bundle: User Pool ID eu-west-1_WG1VW4YTe, Identity Pool ID eu-west-1:6f339b1c-924e-4e71-a751-d32bfe454e74. Both eu-west-1, matching the AppSync endpoint's region.
  • AWS AppSync GraphQL: https://hz5g3vbxy5h2jhpjclyvzfhiju.appsync-api.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/graphql, matched by a validation regex also embedded in the JS bundle: ^https:\/\/\w{26}\.appsync\-api\.\w{2}(?:(?:\-\w{2,})+)\-\d\.amazonaws.com\/graphql$). AWS Amplify/Cognito libraries are bundled (aws-appsync, aws-appsync-auth-link, Cognito identity/idp endpoints for every AWS region). Two literal GraphQL documents were recovered verbatim from the Hermes string table:
query LastData($asset_id: String!) {
  lastData(asset_id: $asset_id) {
    asset_id
    data
  }
}

subscription UpdatedShadow($asset_id: String!, $shadow_name: String) {
  updatedShadow(asset_id: $asset_id, shadow_name: $shadow_name) {
    asset_id
    shadow_name
    data
  }
}

This confirms the app's own cloud layer uses a device-shadow pattern (Redux-slice identifiers desiredList/reported/ deviceDesiredShadow/addDesired/removeDesired also found in the bundle) — commands are likely sent as a GraphQL mutation that patches a "desired" shadow document, reconciled downstream against the real unit. The actual mutation document was not found as a literal string — see Cloud API for why, and what that means for reimplementing it.

  • Gree's own cloud infrastructure is referenced too: grih.gree.com and its regional variants eugrih.gree.com, nagrih.gree.com, hkgrih.gree.com, ingrih.gree.com, megrih.gree.com, sagrih.gree.com, augrih.gree.com, tmpgrih.gree.com (Gree's "GRIH" — Gree Region IoT Hub — cloud servers), plus discovery/routing hosts <region>.dis.gree.com (e.g. ru.dis.gree.com, au.dis.gree.com, in.dis.gree.com, me.dis.gree.com, na.dis.gree.com, sa.dis.gree.com, ts.dis.gree.com, eb.dis.gree.com, hk.dis.gree.com) and *.as.gree.com — bundled as TLS pinning certificates (_.as.gree.com.cer, _.gree.com.cer) and referenced in the native string pool. Whether the app actually talks to these directly, or only through its own AppSync backend, wasn't determined from static analysis alone — that needs live traffic capture.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Notable ones from the app's manifest: BLUETOOTH, BLUETOOTH_SCAN, BLUETOOTH_CONNECT, ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION, NEARBY_WIFI_DEVICES, CHANGE_WIFI_STATE, CHANGE_WIFI_MULTICAST_STATE, ACCESS_WIFI_STATE, CAMERA, NFC — all consistent with BLE/AP-mode WiFi device provisioning (CHANGE_WIFI_MULTICAST_STATE in particular is needed for UDP broadcast discovery on the LAN protocol).

docs.title: Things that were not cracked
docs.text:
• Exact REST/GraphQL paths used by the app's own backend, and the real "send a command" mutation against the AppSync backend — not present as literal strings anywhere in the analyzed build; would require either further static work against obfuscated/minified logic, or capturing live HTTPS traffic (mitmproxy + Frida SSL-unpinning) while using the real app.
  • Whether libgree.so embeds a second, cloud-facing protocol variant or is purely the LAN-protocol crypto helper — no literal endpoint strings in the binary either way.
  • A full Java decompile of the entire app (tens of thousands of classes) was attempted but is extremely slow and wasn't completed/used; all findings above came from targeted string extraction plus the Hermes bundle parse, not a full source dump.

docs.title: Tadirel's architecture
docs.text:
Layout modeled on mon231/vidspy (one shared Python backend, two thin frontends — desktop via Eel, Android via Chaquopy):

backend/                     shared Python core, no UI code in here
  tadiran_ac_backend/
    __init__.py
    protocol_props.py        Props enum + human labels/choices (UI metadata)
    store.py                 JSON-file device store (mac -> ip/mid/name/last_seen)
    arp.py                   cross-platform ARP table lookup (MAC -> IP fallback)
    device.py                thin wrapper around greeclimate.AirConditionerDevice:
                              bind/status/apply, command-confirmation polling
    scanner.py                the "5 probes over 12s, stream new results" scan
    loop_runner.py            shared background asyncio event loop
    api.py                    the ONLY surface both frontends call:
                               start_scan / poll_scan / list_known_devices /
                               set_device_name / rename_device / remove_device /
                               get_status / send_command / capabilities
  requirements.txt

desktop/                     "PC app"
  app.py                     Eel entry point, exposes backend.api functions
                              to JS, opens a native Chrome/Edge app window
  web/
    index.html
    style.css
    app.js                   polls scan, renders device list + control panel
  requirements.txt

app/                         "Android app" (Chaquopy)
  build.gradle               module build file, Chaquopy plugin + python config
  src/main/
    AndroidManifest.xml
    java/com/tadirel/app/
      MainActivity.kt         device list screen (scan/refresh/pair/power)
      DeviceDetailActivity.kt full control screen (mode/temp/fan/swing/...)
      PyBridge.kt              thin Kotlin wrapper: Chaquopy calls into
                                backend.api, JSON in/out
      InsetsUtil.kt            edge-to-edge window inset handling
    python/
      android_bridge.py        Android-only JSON bridge over backend.api
      greeclimate/              vendored copy (see library-notes.md for why)
    res/layout, res/values     native Android views

build.gradle, settings.gradle, gradle.properties, gradlew*   root Gradle wrapper
tests/                        pytest against backend/ only (frontends are thin)
docs/                         this knowledge base (local only, not committed)

docs.title: Why this shape
docs.text:
• One backend, two UIs. All protocol/state logic (scanning, binding, property get/set, the device name store) lives once in backend/tadiran_ac_backend/. Desktop and Android both call the exact same handful of functions in api.py — neither re-implements any networking.
  • Desktop = Eel. Eel runs the Python backend in-process and opens a local web page in an app-mode browser window — gives a "real app" feel with normal HTML/CSS/JS for the UI, zero extra packaging complexity, and is exactly the pattern vidspy/desktop/app.py uses.
  • Android = Chaquopy, native UI. Chaquopy embeds a Python interpreter in the Android app and lets Kotlin call into backend.api directly (JSON strings in, JSON strings out — same shape Eel uses on desktop, so api.py's functions don't need to know which frontend is calling). The UI itself is native Kotlin views (not a WebView), matching vidspy's Android app, which also uses native views with Chaquopy underneath.
  • Scanning contract. scanner.py sends the Gree "scan" probe up to 5 times, once every 2 seconds, while listening continuously; stops entirely at the 12-second mark. Any device reply is reported the instant it arrives (via an internal queue), not batched at the end — both UIs poll that queue every ~300ms while a scan is running so new rows appear live, and both show a "Refresh" action that just starts a new scan.
  • Device identity = MAC. The scan reply's MAC is the stable key for naming/storing a unit (IP can change via DHCP). store.py persists {mac: {ip, mid, name, last_seen}} as local JSON — no server, no cloud account, matches the no-cloud stance from Cloud API.
  • Control screen capabilities are data-driven. protocol_props.py describes each controllable property (label, kind: toggle/enum/int-range, and for enums the choice labels) so both the HTML UI and the native Android UI can render the same control set from one source of truth without hardcoding widgets per platform.
  • Command confirmation, not just send-and-trust. send_command applies the change, then polls the unit's real status until the changed property reads back as requested (or a short timeout elapses) — both UIs show the AC's actual latest state, and warn if it hasn't confirmed yet, rather than assuming success the instant a packet goes out.

docs.title: Device pairing, naming, and liveness
docs.text:
A "pairing" is a user-assigned name attached to a MAC address — this is the only thing that gets persisted to store.py's JSON file. Unnamed scan hits are transient (shown only in the live subnet-scan results while a scan is running); giving one a name is what promotes it into the persisted "known devices" list.

  • Known devices list (always visible, no scan needed to populate it): every {mac: name, ...} entry in the store. Each row shows name, MAC, resolved IP (or "unreachable"), a trash icon (deletes the pairing), and, once a row is selected, an edit icon to rename it.
  • Liveness check for known devices (run on load and on refresh, deliberately cheap — not the full 12s broadcast scan):
  • Unicast a single "scan" probe to the device's last-known IP (~1.5s timeout). A matching reply = alive, update stored IP.
  • If that fails, fall back to an ARP table lookup by MAC to find the current IP (handles DHCP lease changes without re-scanning the whole subnet). If ARP resolves an IP, the device is treated as reachable and the store's IP is updated.
  • If the ARP table has no entry at all for that MAC, the device is marked unreachable: its row is grayed out and cannot be selected for control (the trash icon still works, so a genuinely gone unit can be unpaired).
  • Subnet scan results (the explicit 5-probe/12s broadcast flow) are for finding devices, named or not. A result whose MAC is already in the store shows its existing name; a result with no stored name shows a "Pair" affordance.

docs.title: Explicitly out of scope (for now)
docs.text:
• WiFi/BLE pairing of a brand-new unit (the AP-mode/BLE provisioning flow in Gree's SDK, see App teardown). Tadirel only controls units already joined to the LAN.
  • Tadiran/Gree cloud control (see Cloud API).
  • Tuya-protocol devices — different protocol family, not implemented here.

docs.title: Full asset inventory
docs.text: Exhaustive pass over every asset bundled in the official app: native libraries (all ABIs), the assets/ tree, and a final sweep for third-party SDK identifiers that didn't fit elsewhere. See App teardown for the primary findings and Cloud API for the REST/GraphQL surface — this page is the "everything else" catalog.

docs.title: Native libraries (lib/arm64-v8a/)
docs.text:
Library Size Purpose libgree.so 341 KB Gree AES/crypto primitives (see App teardown) libBleLib.so 16 KB Gree BLE provisioning transport. No literal service/characteristic UUID strings recoverable via static strings — likely stored as raw binary constants, not string literals. libCHIPController.so 10.5 MB Matter/CHIP controller (Tuya's Matter support) — largest native lib in the app by far libThingSmartLink.so 283 KB Tuya ("ThingSmart") WiFi-provisioning SmartLink/SmartConfig native code libthing_security.so 195 KB Tuya SDK crypto/security native layer libthing_security_algorithm.so 77 KB Tuya SDK crypto algorithm implementations libthingmmkv.so 512 KB Tuya's MMKV (Tencent's fast key-value store) bundled for Tuya SDK local storage libVisionCamera.so 276 KB react-native-vision-camera (used for the photo-based AC model recognition feature, see Cloud API's /models/ai/recognize/) libreactnative.so 5.7 MB React Native's own native runtime libhermes.so 2.1 MB Hermes JS engine libhermestooling.so 134 KB Hermes debugging/inspector tooling libjsi.so 382 KB React Native's JS-to-native interface libworklets.so 841 KB react-native-reanimated worklets runtime libreanimated.so 1.4 MB react-native-reanimated libnetwork-android.so 2.3 MB Facebook's native networking stack (Fresco/okhttp-adjacent) libreact_codegen_*.so (4 files) ~1.8 MB total Codegen'd native modules for RNCSlider, rnscreens, rnsvg, safeareacontext librnscreens.so, libgesturehandler.so 101 KB, 38 KB react-native-screens / react-native-gesture-handler libgifimage.so, libimagepipeline.so, libimage_processing_util_jni.so, libnative-filters.so, libnative-imagetranscoder.so ~1 MB combined Fresco image-loading pipeline libfbjni.so 177 KB Facebook's JNI helper library libdatastore_shared_counter.so 7 KB AndroidX DataStore libc++_shared.so 1.3 MB Shared C++ standard library

A strings-level sweep of every .so listed above for URLs/domains found nothing beyond generic toolchain/doc banners (android.googlesource.com, reactnative.dev/docs, perfetto.dev, docs.swmansion.com) — no additional cloud endpoints anywhere in native code. This closes the question raised in earlier passes: networking logic for this app lives entirely in the JS bundle and/or Java/Kotlin layer, never in native code.

docs.title: assets/ tree (base APK)
docs.text: Path Notes index.android.bundle The Hermes-compiled JS bundle — see App teardown for how it was parsed _.as.gree.com.cer, _.gree.com.cer TLS pinning certs for Gree's cloud domains cers Resolved finding: byte-for-byte identical content to thing_domains_v1/regions (below) — both are the same base64-obfuscated Facebook SDK network-pinning blob, bundled twice under different paths by two different RN modules that each vendor a copy. Not AC-related, not a separate discovery. thing_domains_v1/regions, thing_domains_v1/pins, thing_domains_v1/h2.ca.der Despite the "thing" naming (suggesting AWS IoT "Thing"), this is actually Facebook SDK's own TLS-pinning data store, confirmed by the cers duplicate above — a naming coincidence, not an AWS IoT artifact. t_cdc.tcfg Tuya SDK's encrypted device-config blob (file magic bytes coincidentally match an OpenPGP key header; it is not one — opaque, proprietary Tuya format, not decodable without Tuya's own key material) fixed_key.bmp, t_s.bmp Genuine 100×75 24-bit BMP images per file-format inspection (not steganographically disguised data, as far as a surface check can tell) — likely Tuya SDK placeholder/internal assets countryList.en.json Plain country-list data for phone-number/region pickers fonts/ Roboto + "Almoni" (a Hebrew typeface family) weights — confirms Hebrew-market UI design from the font choice alone com/appsflyer/internal/* AppsFlyer SDK's own opaque internal config blobs dexopt/baseline.prof, baseline.profm Android Runtime (ART) baseline profiles for startup optimization, unrelated to app logic

docs.title: Third-party SDK identifiers found
docs.text:
These are client-side identifiers embedded in the shipped app binary — normal for mobile analytics/crash-reporting SDKs (they're not secrets in the security sense; any app installer trivially exposes them, which is why vendors design these SDKs to tolerate public client identifiers). Listed here purely for completeness of the asset inventory:

  • Datadog client token: pub5499c62c9617fe3d0ca63247821a9020. Both datadoghq.com and datadoghq.eu site strings are present (standard Datadog SDK default-option strings) — given every other confirmed backend element is eu-west-1, datadoghq.eu is the more likely active site, but this wasn't independently confirmed.
  • Mixpanel, Firebase, AppsFlyer, Facebook SDK, Emarsys: all present as bundled libraries (consistent with the dependency list implied by app-teardown.md's architecture section), but no static API key/token/project-ID string was recovered with confident attribution for any of them — likely injected via native google-services.json/Gradle resource values rather than plain string literals, or genuinely not present in this build.
  • No Google Maps/Places API key (AIza... pattern) was found anywhere in the dex or JS string pools.

docs.title: What this pass closes out
docs.text:
• Native code confirmed clean of hidden endpoints — every .so in the app was swept; nothing beyond public documentation URLs.
  • The thing_domains_v1 naming red herring is resolved — it is Facebook SDK pinning data, not an AWS IoT Core artifact, confirmed by finding byte-identical content under the unrelated cers path.
  • BLE provisioning UUIDs remain unrecovered — libBleLib.so almost certainly contains them as raw binary GATT UUID bytes rather than ASCII string literals; extracting them would need a disassembler pass on the library itself, not a strings sweep (out of scope here, since this project doesn't implement new-device BLE pairing — see Architecture's "explicitly out of scope" section).

docs.title: The remote/cloud control path — what's known, what isn't, and why Tadirel doesn't use it
docs.text: Short version: it's not publicly documented, and Tadirel deliberately does not reimplement it. Everything below is the research trail, kept for reference in case someone wants to pick it up later. A second pass through the decoded app's JS bundle (see App teardown for how the Hermes bytecode was parsed) turned up a much fuller REST API surface than the first pass found — recorded here.

docs.title: Backend architecture (confirmed)
docs.text:
The app's backend is a hybrid REST + GraphQL + AWS Cognito stack, and — new finding — it's a white-label platform serving more than one HVAC brand: the bundle also contains a complete Ferroli onboarding flow (FerroliConnectFirstScreen, FerroliConnectSecondScreen, ferroliConnectScreen:step1_*/step2_* translation keys). Tadiran's app is one brand's skin on a shared backend/app platform, not a bespoke Tadiran-only system.

  • Auth: AWS Cognito, not a custom login endpoint. Concrete identifiers recovered from the app's native (dex) string pool:
  • Cognito User Pool ID: eu-west-1_WG1VW4YTe
  • Cognito Identity Pool ID: eu-west-1:6f339b1c-924e-4e71-a751-d32bfe454e74
  • Both are eu-west-1, matching the AppSync endpoint's region exactly — strong confirmation these belong to the same backend. No literal App Client ID was found with confidence (one 26-character lowercase alphanumeric candidate, 312eed498hlvku8pdup0lvfpir, sits near version-number strings in the pool with no corroborating context — treat as unconfirmed, not a finding).
  • No custom /login, /signin, /register, /otp, or /refresh paths exist anywhere in the bundle — consistent with auth being handled entirely by the Cognito SDK (SRP login, token refresh, RespondToAuthChallenge/AdminRespondToAuthChallenge are generic AWS SDK symbol names also present, not app-specific endpoints).
  • GraphQL (AWS AppSync): https://hz5g3vbxy5h2jhpjclyvzfhiju.appsync-api.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/graphql. Literal /graphql, /mqtt, and /realtime path strings are all present in the bundle, consistent with AppSync's standard real-time subscription transport (AppSync multiplexes GraphQL subscriptions over an MQTT-over-WebSocket channel). Two literal operations survived Apollo/Amplify's codegen compilation (most queries/mutations get compiled to AST objects, not kept as text — see "What's still missing" below):
query LastData($asset_id: String!) {
  lastData(asset_id: $asset_id) {
    asset_id
    data
  }
}

subscription UpdatedShadow($asset_id: String!, $shadow_name: String) {
  updatedShadow(asset_id: $asset_id, shadow_name: $shadow_name) {
    asset_id
    shadow_name
    data
  }
}

Redux-slice identifiers (deviceDesiredShadow, addDesired, removeDesired, desiredList, reported) confirm a device-shadow pattern: the app writes a "desired" state, something downstream reconciles it against the real unit, "reported" state flows back. - REST API: versioned, brand-prefixed base paths, found as literal strings: - /tadiran-mobile-app/api/v1 - /tadiran-mobile-app/api/v2 - /mobile-app/api/v1 (brand-generic variant/fallback) - /eu/management/api/v1 (a separate "management" subsystem — likely installer/service/warranty tooling, not the consumer app's main surface; activateWarrantyAsyncThunk, application-restriction/, and service/ sit in the same region of the string pool) - Host is presumably api.tadiran-iot.co.il per the earlier pass, but that association wasn't re-confirmed by this pass (the host and the path prefixes never appeared adjacent as one concatenated literal).

docs.title: REST resource paths (literal strings, high confidence)
docs.text:
These appeared as plain path-segment string literals (not Redux action-type names — see the caveat below), most with the trailing slash typical of a REST resource base:

/devices/                          /devices/AC/combined-rules/
/devices/create/                   /devices/AC/grouped-commands/
/devices/schedules/                /devices/schedules/all_rooms/
/devices/shabbat_mode/             /devices/timers/
/devices/tips/                     /devices/quick-actions/
/devices/quick-actions/defaults/   /devices/invitations/
/devices/sub-units/invitations/    /sub-devices/
/sub-units/                        /vrf-box/
/groups/                           /shared-users/
/shared-users/invite/              /shared-users/sub-unit/invite/
/invitations/                      /invitations/accept/
/invitations/reject/               /user/
/user/update/                      /user/consumption-history/
/user/consumption-summary/         /user/fcm-token/update/
/self-profile/                     /self-profile/delete/

Notable ones:

  • /models/ai/recognize/ + /models/ai/upload-image/ — the app can identify an AC model from a photo (upload an image, get a model match).
  • /smart-ir/ — IR-blaster-based "dumb" AC support, a separate path from the WiFi/Gree-protocol device flow this project actually uses.
  • /tadiran-email-check/ — brand-specific (not /mobile-app-email-check/), confirming the white-label platform namespaces at least some endpoints per brand even though most paths are shared.
  • /test-command/ — exists as its own resource, separate from whatever the real device-command endpoint is; possibly a connectivity/dry-run check.

docs.title: Operation inventory (Redux action-type names, lower confidence as URLs)
docs.text:
The bundle is full of createAsyncThunk-style Redux Toolkit action names ending in AsyncThunk, each with /pending, /fulfilled, /rejected suffix variants also present in the pool. These describe operations, not necessarily literal URL paths (a Redux Toolkit thunk's type string is usually "sliceName/thunkName", and Hermes's string deduplication means what we see starting with / could be the tail half of such a type string rather than a URL). Treat this list as "operations that exist", not "endpoints that exist":

getDevicesStatusesAsyncThunk        commandDeviceAsyncThunk
commandBulkSubDeviceAsyncThunk      commandGroupDeviceAsyncThunk
commandDeviceCombinedRuleAsyncThunk addDeviceAsyncThunk
addSubDeviceAsyncThunk              updateDeviceAsyncThunk
deleteDeviceAsyncThunk              getDeviceOtaStatusAsyncThunk
getSubDeviceShadowAsyncThunk        getSubDevicesShadowAsyncThunk
discoverVrfBoxDevicesAsuncThunk     getVrfBoxDevicesAsuncThunk
getACModelsAsyncThunk               getACModelBySerialNumber
addUserAsyncThunk                   getUserAsyncThunk
getMyUsersAsyncThunk                deleteUserAsyncThunk
patchUserAsyncThunk                 getSelfProfileDataAsyncThunk
deleteSharedUserAsyncThunk          deleteSharedUserDevicesAsyncThunk
activateDeviceScheduleAsyncThunk    createDeviceScheduleAsyncThunk
deleteSelectedDeviceScheduleAsyncThunk
updateSelectedDeviceScheduleAsyncThunk
getDevicesSchedulesAsyncThunk       getAllRoomsSchedulesAsyncThunk
setSelectedDeviceTimerAsyncThunk    deleteSelectedDeviceTimer
updateSelectedDeviceTimerAsyncThunk getDevicesTimersAsyncThunk
fetchDeviceQuestionnaire            patchDeviceQuestionnaire
fetchConsumptionHistoryAsyncThunk   fetchConsumptionSummaryAsyncThunk
getQuickActionsAsyncThunk           upsertQuickActionAsyncThunk
deleteQuickActionAsyncThunk         signOutAsyncThunk
rateTipAsyncThunk                   getTipsAsyncThunk
setFiltersReminderAsyncThunk        activateWarrantyAsyncThunk
setSmartIRFetchedInfo

(Shabbat-mode scheduling — fetchShabbatTimeDataAsyncThunk, setShabbatModeStatusAndLocationAsyncThunk, and about a dozen related thunks — is a real, fairly elaborate feature: AC schedules that respect Shabbat/holiday timing rules, specific to the Israeli market.)

docs.title: Transport/header hints
docs.text: Literal strings Authorization, x-api-key, Content-Type, BASE_URL, baseURL/baseUrl all exist in the bundle. These are generic HTTP client symbol names (the kind any fetch/axios-based API client would reference), not proof of specific header values — no actual API key or bearer token format was recovered.

docs.title: What's still missing
docs.text:
• The actual command request/response shape: which REST path takes the Gree protocol command, what JSON body it expects (raw Pow/Mod/ SetTem-style keys? Tuya-style {"code": ..., "value": ...} DPs, given the app also bundles Tuya's SDK? Something else entirely?), and what HTTP method it uses. /test-command/ and commandDeviceAsyncThunk exist, but their payload format wasn't recoverable from static strings.
  • The GraphQL mutation that writes to the device shadow (the write-side of the shadow pattern) — not found as a literal string; almost certainly compiled to an AST object by Apollo/Amplify codegen rather than kept as text, same as most other GraphQL operations here.
  • Request authentication details beyond "it's Cognito" — no App Client ID confirmed, no observed token format, no confirmation of whether REST calls carry a Cognito ID token, access token, or an AppSync-style API key via x-api-key.
  • Whether commands reach the unit via Gree's own cloud (grih.gree.com and regional variants, *.dis.gree.com, bundled as TLS-pinned hosts — see App teardown), via the vendor's own Lambda-behind-AppSync/REST layer, or some hybrid of both.

docs.title: Public reverse-engineering landscape
docs.text:
Checked for existing community work on Gree's cloud API specifically:

  • The LAN protocol is thoroughly documented and has multiple independent open-source implementations (see LAN protocol).
  • The cloud/remote protocol is not. Multiple long-running Home Assistant / SmartThings / openHAB community threads about Gree integrations explicitly say the cloud side is essentially undocumented ("pretty hard to get any documentation for the EWPE/gree.com cloud"). No public openapi.gree.com, no public OAuth flow, no community client library for it exists, unlike the LAN side.
  • The vendor's own IoT backend has zero public footprint — no developer portal, nothing indexed, despite now having a much fuller picture of its URL surface than a typical "zero public footprint" API would suggest existed.

docs.title: Why Tadirel doesn't chase it further
docs.text:
1. It would still require capturing live HTTPS traffic from the real app (mitmproxy + Frida SSL-unpinning on a rooted/emulated device) to see actual request/response bodies — the path names are now known, but not a single full request/response pair, auth header, or payload shape.
  2. Even captured, it'd depend on Cognito-issued, presumably short-lived auth tokens tied to a real account — fragile to reimplement and maintain compared to the LAN protocol, which needs no account at all.
  3. It is not demonstrably "open and free to use" the way the LAN protocol is — nothing here confirms the vendor's actual terms bless third-party reimplementation of their private cloud API.
  4. The actual goal — "control my own AC, including from outside my house" — is fully achievable by tunneling into the LAN (Tailscale/ WireGuard) and using the local protocol, with none of the above risk. That's the path Tadirel takes; see Architecture.

docs.title: If someone wants to pick this up anyway
docs.text: Now that real path names exist, the lowest-risk next static step (still short of live traffic capture) would be probing which of these paths resolve on api.tadiran-iot.co.il with an unauthenticated OPTIONS or GET request (e.g. /config/ sounds like exactly the kind of endpoint an app would call before authenticating, to fetch its own AWS Amplify config — which would hand over the App Client ID this pass couldn't confirm). Beyond that, the concrete next step is still: install the app on a device you can MITM (or an emulator + Frida), trigger a real "send command" action while on mobile data (not WiFi, to force it through the cloud path rather than Tadirel's own LAN path), and capture the actual request. Once you have one real request, the bind-time local key (see LAN protocol) is worth testing as a decryption key for any encrypted payload field in that request/response — the local and cloud paths plausibly reuse the same per-device key for their respective pack-style payloads, though this is unverified speculation, not a confirmed finding.

docs.title: The Gree "Gree+" LAN protocol (what Tadirel actually uses)
docs.text:
This is the open, community-documented protocol spoken by the AC's WiFi module over your local network. It needs no account, no internet, and no vendor server — just UDP connectivity to the unit on your subnet. Tadirel's backend talks this protocol via the greeclimate PyPI library (the same one Home Assistant's gree integration uses).

References: tomikaa87/gree-remote, cmroche/greeclimate.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text:
• UDP, port 7000 on the AC's WiFi module.
  • Every message is a JSON object. Most messages carry an encrypted pack field (base64 AES ciphertext of another JSON object) plus envelope fields:
{"t": "pack", "i": 0, "uid": 0, "cid": "<mac>", "tcid": "",
 "pack": "<base64 AES ciphertext>"}

(bind/scan requests use "i": 1 and a fixed "generic" key; everything after binding uses "i": 0 and the per-device key returned by bind.)

docs.title: Message flow
docs.text:
1. Scan — broadcast (or unicast) {"t": "scan"} to 255.255.255.255:7000 (or a specific IP). Any unit on the network replies with its identity (pack.t == "dev"), containing at least cid (MAC), mac, name, brand, model, ver, mid — encrypted with the generic key.
  2. Bind — send a bind request (pack.t == "bind", containing mac), encrypted with the generic key. The unit replies (pack.t == "bindok") with a device-specific key — this is the "local key" value Tadirel reports after binding. All further messages to that unit use this key instead of the generic one.
  3. Status — send {"t":"status", "cols":["Pow","Mod","SetTem",...]} (encrypted). Reply pack.t == "dat" contains cols + dat (parallel arrays) with current values.
  4. Command — send {"t":"cmd", "opt":[...names...], "p":[...values...]} (encrypted). Reply pack.t == "res" echoes back the applied values.

There is no persistent "connection" — it's simple request/reply UDP. Replies arrive asynchronously (via the OS socket's receive callback), so code that sends a request and immediately reads local state without waiting a beat will see nothing (greeclimate's send() explicitly documents "completion does not imply a reply" — see Library notes).

docs.title: Keys and ciphers
docs.text:
Two cipher variants exist in the wild (greeclimate tries V1, falls back to V2 automatically):

  • CipherV1 — AES-128-ECB, PKCS7 padding. Generic/default key used for scan+bind: a3K8Bx%2r8Y7#xDh (ASCII, 16 bytes). This is the well-known public "Gree generic key" published by every open-source Gree project; it is not secret and is the same across every Gree-protocol device worldwide — it isn't tied to any individual unit or account, it's a shared bootstrap key the protocol uses before a per-device key is negotiated.
  • CipherV2 — AES-128-GCM. Some newer firmware/WiFi modules only speak this even for the initial scan reply. Fixed values observed in the library/protocol: generic key {yxAHAY_Lm6pbC/< (16 bytes), GCM nonce 54 40 78 44 49 67 5a 51 6c 5e 63 13 (12 bytes), and additional authenticated data (AAD) qualcomm-test.

The per-device key obtained at bind time replaces the generic key for everything after binding, under whichever cipher version the unit actually negotiated. This per-device key is not secret either in any meaningful sense — it's handed to any client on the LAN that completes the public bind handshake with the unit; it just scopes subsequent messages to that one device rather than authenticating a user.

docs.title: Property keys (Props in greeclimate.air_conditioner)
docs.text:
These are the literal JSON keys sent/received in cols/opt and dat/p. Confirmed present as literal strings in the official Tadiran app's own binary for at least Pow, Lig, Tur (see App teardown) — strong direct evidence Tadiran units speak this exact protocol, not just "something Gree-like".

Key Meaning Values Pow Power 0 off / 1 on Mod Mode 0 auto, 1 cool, 2 dry, 3 fan, 4 heat SetTem Target temperature integer, see TemRec/TemUn below TemUn Temperature unit 0 Celsius, 1 Fahrenheit TemRec Temperature "recommend" bit fine-grained encoding alongside SetTem for half-degree F precision; greeclimate manages this automatically TemSen Current temperature sensor reading integer, decoded via TemRec/TemUn WdSpd Fan speed 0 auto, 1–5 (low→high) Air Fresh air / "Air" valve 0/1 Blo X-Fan (blow residual moisture out after cooling/dry) 0/1 Health Anion/health/ionizer 0/1 SwhSlp Sleep mode 0/1 (paired with SlpMod) SlpMod Sleep mode (secondary flag) 0/1 Lig Display light / LED 0/1 SwingLfRig Horizontal swing / louver position integer enum (unit-dependent) SwUpDn Vertical swing / louver position integer enum (unit-dependent) Quiet Quiet mode 0 off, 2 on (not 1 — greeclimate encodes this) Tur Turbo mode 0/1 StHt Steady heat (8°C heating) 0/1 SvSt Power save mode 0/1 HeatCoolType Unknown/unused heat-cool type flag present in some firmware, not exposed via a greeclimate setter

Valid target temperature range (Celsius): 8–30 °C.

docs.title: Confirmed working live
docs.text: Scanned a real home LAN and found 4 real units (all mid=10001, UDP port 7000). Round-tripped a real status read and a real power on→off cycle against one of them — bound, read status (power/mode/target+current temp/fan speed), toggled power on, verified via a second status read, then restored it to its original state.

docs.title: greeclimate library notes (found while building against real hardware)
docs.text: Package: greeclimate on PyPI (v4.3.0 used here). Async (asyncio), used by Home Assistant's gree integration. Modules used by backend/: greeclimate.discovery.Discovery, greeclimate.device_factory.create_device, greeclimate.air_conditioner.AirConditionerDevice/Props, greeclimate.cipher.CipherV1, greeclimate.deviceinfo.DeviceInfo.

docs.title: Quirks that actually mattered (desktop)
docs.text:
1. send() does not wait for a reply. Device.send()'s own docstring says "completion does not imply a reply" — it only waits for the local socket write to drain. The actual reply arrives later via datagram_received(). Reading a property (device.power, etc.) right after await device.update_state() or await device.push_state_update() with no delay will see stale/None data. Fix: always await asyncio.sleep(~1) after update_state()/push_state_update() before reading properties.

  2. device.bind(key=..., cipher=...) does not open a transport. Its docstring says so explicitly ("does not open a transport"), and its implementation just sets self.device_cipher = cipher and returns. Calling any send afterwards raises DeviceNotBoundError because _ensure_bound() only (re)binds if not self.device_cipher — and a manually-set cipher makes it think it's already fully bound. Tadirel's backend always does a fresh full bind per interaction rather than trying to cache/reuse the per-device key across process runs via this method — it's cheap (one local UDP round-trip, not a network call) and avoids the issue entirely.

  3. Discovery vs. per-IP bind both need DeviceInfo. create_device() needs a populated DeviceInfo (ip, port, mac, name, mid) to pick the right device class (dispatch is by mid, see greeclimate.device_factory.DEVICE_TYPES/KNOWN_MID_PROFILES). You can either get one from Discovery.scan() (broadcast or unicast) or construct one directly if you already know those fields from a previous scan, skipping the multi-second scan wait entirely. Tadirel's device store caches mid specifically so later unicast health-checks/binds can skip rediscovery.

  4. Windows note (asyncio.windows_events). Running discovery across multiple local network interfaces (VPN/virtual adapters with no real route) throws harmless OSError: [WinError 1231] The network location cannot be reached from ProactorEventLoop's internals — caught per-interface by asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True) inside Discovery.search_devices(), so it doesn't break the scan; it just prints noise to stderr. Safe to ignore.

  5. Enum encodings worth knowing:

  6. quiet setter maps True → 2, False → 0 (not 1) — reading back Props.QUIET as a plain int for display should treat any non-zero value as "on".
  7. target_temperature with temperature_units == 1 (Fahrenheit) writes two properties together (SetTem + TemRec) for half-degree precision — always set/read them as a pair, never SetTem alone, when Fahrenheit is in play. Tadirel always runs in Celsius (TemUn = 0) to avoid the complication.
  8. sleep setter writes both SwhSlp and SlpMod together.

docs.title: Getting it running on Android (Chaquopy)
docs.text:
Three real problems showed up getting this library running on an actual device — none of them in Tadirel's own backend code, which was already validated against real hardware from the desktop app first:

  1. greeclimate isn't really pip-installable for Android. Chaquopy's package mirror only had greeclimate up to a very old 2.x release, which predates the modern API this project is built against entirely (different module layout, no AirConditionerDevice/Props/ device_factory). Fix: vendor the real, modern greeclimate source as plain Python files in the Android app rather than pip-installing it at all.

!!! warning "License" greeclimate is GPLv3-licensed. Vendoring its source is fine for personal/sideloaded builds, but re-check GPL source-availability obligations before distributing a built APK to anyone else.

  1. Chaquopy's pycryptodome wheel for Android is broken. Its cross-compiled arm64-v8a wheels are missing native cipher extension modules (Crypto.Util._cpuid_c on newer releases, Crypto.Cipher ._raw_ecb even on older ones) — every version crashed the app at startup with OSError: Cannot load native module. Fix: the Android build's vendored cipher.py uses javax.crypto (part of the Android platform itself, reached via Chaquopy's Java interop) instead of pycryptodome — same AES-128-ECB and AES-128-GCM semantics as upstream, zero native-wheel risk. The desktop app is unaffected; it still uses real pycryptodome via normal desktop Python, which works fine there.

  2. PEP 604 X | None annotations crash on older Python runtimes. Modern greeclimate was written against Python 3.10+, which evaluates str | None as an actual runtime expression in a function signature. An older on-device Python interpreter doesn't support that syntax at runtime, and crashes with TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'type' and 'NoneType' the moment the affected module is imported. Fix: from __future__ import annotations at the top of every vendored module (defers all annotations to strings, never evaluated at runtime) — a no-op everywhere else, a required fix here.

docs.title: Capability discovery
docs.text: AirConditionerDevice._capability_names lists what the class can expose (power, mode, target_temperature, temperature_units, current_temperature, fan_speed, fresh_air, xfan, anion, sleep, light, horizontal_swing, vertical_swing, quiet, turbo, steady_heat, power_save, buzzer_control) — but that's a static class-level list, not a live capability negotiation with the actual unit. Real per-unit capabilities come back as whatever columns the unit actually answers a status request with. Tadirel's UI renders controls for the full static property list and simply shows "—" for anything the unit doesn't report a value for.
